notes:
Task and constraints: Update a Minesweeper board after a click, revealing adjacent mine counts or recursively blank regions.
Idea: Use a queue of cells to reveal, count neighboring mines, and enqueue adjacent unrevealed cells when the count is zero.
Technique and why it applies: A clicked mine becomes X immediately. Otherwise a cell with neighboring mines becomes its digit; a cell with none becomes B and its neighboring E cells are marked with a space before being queued to prevent duplicate enqueues.
Invariant: Cells in the next queue are newly discovered cells whose neighbors still need to be examined.
Edge cases: The code assumes click is inside a nonempty rectangular board. Marking queued cells as a literal space is an internal visited marker that differs from the usual board alphabet until that cell is processed.
Complexity: Each cell is queued at most once and checks eight neighbors, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case queue space.

Task and constraints: Reveal the Minesweeper board after a click, following the mine-count and blank-expansion rules.
Idea: Use an explicit stack to perform depth-first expansion from the clicked cell.
Technique and why it applies: If the click is a mine, it is marked X. Otherwise each popped cell counts adjacent mines; a nonzero count becomes a digit, while a zero count becomes B and its still-E neighbors are marked as spaces and pushed.
Invariant: Every stack entry is a discovered cell awaiting its adjacent mine count; marking E neighbors before pushing prevents duplicate visits.
Edge cases: The code assumes a valid click and a nonempty rectangular board. The temporary space marker is replaced when that cell is popped.
Complexity: Each cell is processed at most once with constant eight-neighbor work, so time is O(RC) and worst-case stack space is O(RC).

Task and constraints: Count unique pairs of values with absolute difference k in nums.
Idea: Sort the values and use a dictionary of values shifted by k to detect when a matching larger value appears.
Technique and why it applies: For each n, dict1 stores n+k as a key. When the current value already exists as a key, some earlier value was exactly k smaller; the result list is deduplicated before its length is returned.
Invariant: dict1 contains keys corresponding to earlier values plus k, so a hit identifies a pair ending at the current value.
Edge cases: For k=0, duplicate values trigger hits and set conversion counts each value once, matching the zero-difference interpretation. The code assumes k is nonnegative as in the problem.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n); dictionary processing is O(n) expected, and result/set storage is O(n).

Task and constraints: Count distinct pairs whose values differ by exactly k.
Idea: Track values already seen and add the smaller or current value to a result set when the matching partner is present.
Technique and why it applies: If num-k is in lookup, num is the larger endpoint and the smaller value is added. If num+k is in lookup, num is the smaller endpoint and is added. A set prevents duplicate pairs from being counted repeatedly.
Invariant: lookup contains all previously scanned values, while result contains distinct smaller endpoints of valid pairs.
Edge cases: Negative k returns zero immediately. With k=0, a value is added when a duplicate has already appeared, and result counts each duplicated value once.
Complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the lookup and result sets.

Task and constraints: Multiply two complex numbers represented as strings such as a+bi and return the product in the same format.
Idea: Parse each real and imaginary component, then apply the complex multiplication formula.
Technique and why it applies: (a+bi)(x+yi) has real part ax-by and imaginary part ay+bx because i²=-1. The code extracts components around '+' and the trailing i, calculates both parts, and concatenates the output.
Invariant: a and b hold the first number's real and imaginary parts, while x and y hold the second's.
Edge cases: The expected input format includes a plus sign and trailing i. Negative imaginary parts are represented in the substring after '+', which int can parse, though alternate sign formatting would need matching input structure.
Complexity: Parsing and arithmetic take O(n) time in the input-string lengths, and the output string uses O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the product of two complex numbers encoded as strings.
Idea: Split each string into integer real and imaginary parts and compute the standard product.
Technique and why it applies: The real component is ra*rb - ia*ib and the imaginary component is ra*ib + ia*rb. Formatting both integers as '%d+%di' yields the requested representation.
Invariant: The parsed pairs (ra,ia) and (rb,ib) preserve the values of the two input complex numbers.
Edge cases: The code expects a trailing i and a plus separator, consistent with the problem format. Negative component text can still be parsed by int after splitting at the plus sign when the sign belongs to the second component.
Complexity: Parsing, multiplication, and formatting take O(n) time in the string lengths, with O(n) space for the returned string.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum circular time difference between any two clock times.
Idea: Convert each time to minutes after midnight, sort the values, and compare adjacent differences plus the wraparound gap.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting makes the minimum non-wraparound gap occur between adjacent values. The circular gap from the last time to the first on the next day is also considered by adding 1440 minutes.
Invariant: min_diff is the smallest gap among adjacent sorted times processed so far, then is updated with the wraparound gap.
Edge cases: Duplicate time points produce a zero adjacent difference. The code assumes at least one time point because it indexes the first and last sorted entries.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), the scan is O(n), and the converted minute list uses O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the one value that appears once in a sorted array where every other value appears exactly twice.
Idea: Recursively split the array in half, remove a matching pair that straddles the split if present, then keep the half with odd length.
Technique and why it applies: After removing the pair across the boundary, the unique value must lie in the half containing an odd number of remaining elements, because all paired values contribute even counts.
Invariant: Each recursive input is a sorted segment containing exactly one singleton and all other values paired.
Edge cases: A one-element segment returns that element as a list, and the caller selects its first element. The snippet has mixed tab/space indentation in comments; if that indentation is preserved inconsistently, Python can raise TabError.
Complexity: Each level slices and processes the array, leading to O(n) total copying work across geometric-sized subarrays, with O(log n) recursion depth for balanced halves.

Task and constraints: Reverse the first k characters of every block of 2k characters in string s.
Idea: Convert s to a list and reverse the slice beginning at every 2k-th position.
Technique and why it applies: Reversing s[i:i+k] affects the first half of each 2k block; the next k characters are left unchanged because the loop advances by 2k.
Invariant: Before each iteration, all earlier 2k blocks have had their first k characters reversed and all remaining characters are unchanged.
Edge cases: A final block shorter than k is reversed entirely, while a block between k and 2k reverses only its first k characters. The debug print emits the character list as a side effect.
Complexity: The slices and reversals touch each character a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(n) list space.

Task and constraints: Reverse the first k characters in each 2k-character segment of s, leaving the next k unchanged.
Idea: Convert the string to a mutable list and reverse the first k slice at every 2k interval.
Technique and why it applies: The loop positions are 0, 2k, 4k, and so on. Replacing each slice with its reversed iterator changes exactly the required prefix of each segment.
Invariant: All blocks before the current index have been transformed correctly, and the suffix starting at i is still in its original order.
Edge cases: Python slicing naturally handles a final segment shorter than k or between k and 2k characters. The method assumes k is positive under the constraints.
Complexity: Each character participates in at most one reversal, so time is O(n). The list representation uses O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: For each cell in a binary matrix, return its distance to the nearest zero using four-directional movement.
Idea: Initialize all zero cells as BFS sources and set nonzero cells to a large provisional distance.
Technique and why it applies: Multi-source BFS expands outward from all zeros. A neighbor is updated only if the distance through the current cell is smaller than its existing value, so the first shortest-distance layers propagate across the matrix.
Invariant: Each queued cell has a finalized or improved distance, and every update extends a known distance by one.
Edge cases: Empty matrices or an empty first row return an empty list. The snippet uses deque without importing it, so deque must be available externally or execution fails.
Complexity: BFS visits cells and their four neighbors, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) queue space. The method modifies mat in place and returns it.

Task and constraints: Compute the distance of every matrix cell to the nearest zero.
Idea: Use two dynamic-programming passes, first from top-left to bottom-right and then in reverse order.
Technique and why it applies: The first pass considers paths entering from above and left; the second incorporates paths from below and right. Together these directions cover shortest Manhattan paths from any cell to a zero.
Invariant: After the first pass, dp contains best distances using top/left approaches; after the reverse pass, each state also considers bottom/right approaches.
Edge cases: The code assumes matrix has at least one row and one column. If no zero exists, entries remain infinity because no finite source distance is available.
Complexity: Both passes scan every cell, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) auxiliary space for dp. The collections import is unused.

Task and constraints: Return the nearest-zero distance for every cell in a binary matrix.
Idea: Initialize every zero as a source in a queue and propagate distances to neighboring cells by BFS.
Technique and why it applies: Ones are initialized to infinity. Whenever a neighbor can be assigned a smaller distance than its current value, it is updated to the current distance plus one and enqueued.
Invariant: Each finite matrix entry is a discovered path length from some zero, and updates only decrease that distance.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty matrix because it indexes matrix[0]. If the matrix contains no zero, all cells remain infinity.
Complexity: Each successful update may enqueue a cell, and distances decrease toward the shortest path; for the multi-source BFS structure this is O(RC) time and O(RC) queue space. The matrix is modified in place.

Task and constraints: Find each cell's Manhattan distance to the nearest zero in the matrix.
Idea: Perform a forward and backward dynamic-programming pass directly on the input matrix.
Technique and why it applies: In the forward pass, each nonzero cell considers its top and left neighbors. In the reverse pass, it considers bottom and right neighbors, allowing shortest paths approaching from all directions to contribute.
Invariant: Each pass lowers nonzero entries when a neighboring route yields a shorter distance; zeros remain fixed at zero.
Edge cases: The method assumes a nonempty rectangular matrix. If there is no zero, values become infinity and remain so because no finite distance source exists.
Complexity: Two full scans give O(RC) time and O(1) auxiliary space because distances are stored in the input matrix.

Task and constraints: Maximize points from removing contiguous groups of equal-colored boxes, earning the square of each removed group size.
Idea: Use memoized interval DP with state (i,j,k), where k same-colored boxes are carried alongside the left endpoint.
Technique and why it applies: One option removes B[i] together with its k carried boxes immediately. Another option delays that group until a matching color at m can be joined, first clearing the intervening interval; the better score is retained.
Invariant: dp(i,j,k) is the maximum score obtainable from B[i:j+1] when k same-colored boxes are attached to B[i].
Edge cases: An empty interval returns zero. The code uses lru_cache without importing it in the snippet, so it needs to be defined externally or execution fails.
Complexity: The memoized state space is O(n³), and each state may scan O(n) matching positions, giving O(n⁴) worst-case time and O(n³) cache space.

Task and constraints: Maximize the score obtained by removing same-colored contiguous box groups, with score equal to group size squared.
Idea: Memoize a recursive interval state and compress any same-colored run at the left edge into the carried count k.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence either removes the left run now or delays it to merge with a matching box later, after clearing the intervening range. The three-dimensional lookup stores results for interval endpoints and carried count.
Invariant: dfs(boxes,l,r,k) returns the best score for the interval while k extra boxes matching boxes[l] are already grouped with its left edge.
Edge cases: l>r returns zero. The lookup uses zero as the uncached sentinel; valid nonempty states have positive score, so computed values are reusable. The input boxes is not modified.
Complexity: There are O(n³) possible states and each may scan O(n) positions, giving O(n⁴) worst-case time and O(n³) memo space.

Task and constraints: Count connected groups of cities in the symmetric adjacency matrix.
Idea: Build an adjacency list and use DFS to visit all cities reachable from each unvisited city.
Technique and why it applies: Each unvisited city starts a new province count; DFS explores its connected neighbors and marks them visited so they are not counted as separate provinces.
Invariant: visit contains cities reached from the current DFS traversal, and count is the number of connected components started so far.
Edge cases: The code uses defaultdict without importing it in this snippet, so that name must be supplied externally. Isolated cities have no adjacency-list entry and are still counted once by the outer loop.
Complexity: Building the graph costs O(n²), and DFS visits each city and connection at most once, for O(n²) total time and O(n²) adjacency storage.

Task and constraints: Decide whether an attendance record is eligible, with fewer than two absences and no three consecutive late marks.
Idea: Scan for any LLL substring and count occurrences of A, rejecting the record if either rule is violated.
Technique and why it applies: Every three-character window is checked for LLL, and the second pass counts absences. The boolean remains true only when both conditions are satisfied.
Invariant: eligible records whether any forbidden late run has been found; absent is the number of absences counted so far.
Edge cases: Strings shorter than three skip the late-run loop. Exactly one absence is allowed, while two or more make the result false.
Complexity: Two linear scans give O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Check that a student's attendance record contains at most one A and never has three consecutive L characters.
Idea: Scan once, count absences, and immediately reject a second absence or a triple of consecutive lates.
Technique and why it applies: The absence count catches the first forbidden condition. At each index with two following characters available, equality of all three characters to L catches the other condition.
Invariant: count_A is the number of absences seen in the prefix, and no violation has been found before the current index if the loop continues.
Edge cases: A record of length below three cannot contain LLL, and a single A is allowed. Early returns stop scanning as soon as a violation is detected.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count attendance records of length n with at most one absence and no three consecutive late days, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Model valid suffix states as a six-state transition system and use binary exponentiation of its transition matrix.
Technique and why it applies: The adjacency matrix encodes how each state transitions when P, A, or L is appended. Raising it to n and multiplying by the initial-state vector counts the valid records ending in each state; the entries are summed modulo MODULUS.
Invariant: power(A,exp) returns the transition matrix raised to exp, with modular reduction after each multiplication.
Edge cases: The snippet depends on NumPy and uses int64 matrix multiplication; under the fixed six-state matrix and modulus, products of reduced entries fit within signed 64-bit range for these operations. n=0 would return one empty record.
Complexity: Matrix exponentiation takes O(log n) multiplications of fixed 6x6 matrices, so O(log n) time and O(1) space with respect to n, aside from NumPy arrays.
